results.quote: There is an algorithm that sorts a \(\pi\)-avoiding sequence S of length n in \(O((logc_\pi+1)\cdot n)\) time even if \(\pi\) is a priori unknown.
There is a comparison-based algorithm that sorts a permutation of length n and twin-with d in \(O(d\cdot n)\) time even if d is a priori unknown.
Any comparison-based sorting algorithm must make at least \(\Omega((logc_\pi+1)\cdot n)\) comparisons in the worst case on \(\pi\)-avoiding sequences.

There is an algorithm that receives on input a \(\pi\)-avoiding sequence S of length n partitioned into m presorted sequences S_1,...,S_m with \(m\le\frac{n}{\mathrm{log}n}\), and outputs S sorted in \(O((\mathrm{log}c_\pi+1)\cdot n)\) time even if \(\pi\) is a priori unknown.

Let S_1,...,S_{n/k} be \(\pi\)-avoiding sequences, each of length k. Then there is an algorithm that sorts all S_i's in time \(O((\mathrm{log}c_\pi+1)\cdot n)+2^{2^{O(k\mathrm{log}k)}}\) even if \(\pi\) is a priori unknown.
